item.title: TheHive/Cortex - v5.0.0 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
# v5.0.0 - "The Hive Inspection" Major release. Same commands, alert actions and parameters, but several behaviours were wrong and are now corrected, which changes what you see. ## Compatibility | | Minimum | Tested with | | :------ | :----------------------- | :---------------- | | TheHive | 5.2.0 | 5.8.1 | | Cortex | 3.0.0 | 4.2.0 | | Splunk | 9.3 (Python 3.9 or 3.13) | Enterprise 10.2.1 | ## Before you upgrade 1. **Sourcetypes of the add-on logs.** 23 of 27 log files had no sourcetype since v4.0.0. The fix needs a manual step: in `$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/learned/local/props.conf`, remove every stanza whose source is a `TA-thehive-cortex_*.log` or `*_modalert.log` file, then restart Splunk. Events indexed before the upgrade keep their old sourcetype; to search both, use `index=_internal source=*TA-thehive-cortex_*.log`. 2. **The datatypes lookup moved to the KV store.** `| inputlookup thehive_datatypes` is unchanged; drop the `.csv` from `| inputlookup thehive_datatypes.csv`. Existing rows are migrated on the first alert action after the upgrade. 3. **Fifteen log identifiers changed** (each designated two events at once). A correspondence table is in the full release notes. 4. **Dashboard CREATE dropdowns** now have sensible defaults instead of creating CRITICAL, TLP:WHITE objects. Alert actions are unaffected. ## Fixed * The three Cortex commands could not run in v4.2.2. * `cortexjobs` no longer confuses "running" with "empty". * The Cortex job action sent its TLP and PAP one level too high. * Cortex ignored the configured CA bundle. * The `TheHive: Statistics` and `TheHive: Alerts` dashboards displayed nothing; `Audit Logs` had three panels querying a sourcetype never produced. * Alert actions reported success as failure; a refused TTP no longer fails an alert that was created. * Two debug lines wrote credentials into the logs. ## New * Settings: **HTTP Timeout (seconds)** and **Cortex Job Max Wait (seconds)**. * The Audit view refreshes itself. Full release notes: see `release_notes/v5.0.0.md` in the repository.


Description:
This TA allows to add interaction features between TheHive or Cortex (https://www.strangebee.com/) and Splunk. It allows to retrieve all kind of information from TheHive/Cortex and to perform actions on these instances using Splunk, from a search or from a predefined dashboard. This TA is supporting only TheHive 5. For having an app supporting TheHive 3 or 4, please check the oldest releases. It's also supporting the Cortex 3 version. More information here: https://github.com/LetMeR00t/TA-thehive-cortex

item.title: ROVIX Universal API Add-on for Splunk - v1.0.3 [New App Release]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
Version 1.0.3 - reliability and bug-fix release Fixes \- Cursor pagination no longer stops early when the API returns a cursor value of 0. \- Malformed Retry-After headers no longer stop collection. \- {{checkpoint}} and other placeholders are now URL-encoded in the URL and form-encoded in form bodies (fixes timestamps with "+" offsets). \- JSON bodies with unquoted placeholders, e.g. {"min_id": {{checkpoint}}}, are now accepted; an empty value is sent as null. \- Short-lived OAuth tokens (under 60 seconds) are reused instead of being requested before every call. \- Temporary token-endpoint errors (429, 5xx, network) are retried automatically. \- Very large numeric IDs are stored exactly (no rounding). \- If a page fails partway through a run, events already collected are not collected again (oldest-first APIs). \- Checkpoints keep working when KV Store is disabled or unavailable (local file fallback). \- Windows: token refresh no longer times out when two inputs share an account. \- License notices no longer reappear in Splunk Messages on every run. Improvements \- Warning in the logs when the Events path is not found, listing the fields the API returned. \- Fewer token-store lookups per run. \- Python settings updated for Splunk 10.2 and later; earlier versions remain supported. Upgrade: install over the previous version. Accounts, inputs, checkpoints and license keys are kept.


Short Description:
Collects data from any REST or JSON API through a modular input with comprehensive authentication support, configurable pagination, and KV Store checkpointing.


Description:
ROVIX Universal API Add-on for Splunk lets you bring data from any REST/JSON API into Splunk by filling in forms. No code or custom scripts are needed. The problem it solves Security and IT teams need data from dozens of cloud services: identity providers, EDR tools, SaaS platforms, threat-intelligence feeds and internal APIs. Many of these have no Splunk add-on, or the add-on is outdated or limited. The usual workarounds are custom Python scripts or one-off modular inputs. Each one handles OAuth tokens, pagination and “what did I already collect?” differently, breaks when a token expires, and is hard to maintain or hand over. What the add-on does One place for every API. Define an account (credentials and authentication) once, then create as many inputs as you need. Each input has its own endpoint, interval, index and sourcetype. Handles authentication for you. Supports OAuth 2.0 (client credentials, authorization code with automatic refresh-token rotation, password grant), JWT bearer and private_key_jwt (including Google service accounts), session login, HMAC request signing, API key, bearer token, Basic and Digest, plus mTLS. Tokens are stored encrypted in Splunk, refreshed before they expire, and renewed automatically if the API rejects them. Collects everything, exactly once. Built-in pagination (offset, page, cursor, Link header, next URL) fetches every page. Checkpoints in the KV Store pick up where the last run stopped, and only move forward after a run completes successfully, so data isn’t skipped. Built to keep running. Retries with back-off on rate limits (HTTP 429) and server errors, honouring Retry-After. A monitoring dashboard and per-input logs make problems easy to see. Who it’s for: Splunk admins and SOC teams who need to onboard API-based data sources quickly and reliably on Splunk Enterprise or Splunk Cloud Platform, without writing and maintaining code. Licensing: a 30-day free evaluation with all features is included, then a per-server license key, verified offline. The add-on runs entirely inside your Splunk environment and sends no data to Rovix Technologies. Developed by Rovix Technologies Pvt. Ltd. Contact: info@RovixTechnologies.com

item.title: Splunk MCP Server - v2.1.0 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
**Splunk MCP Server 2.1.0** Splunk MCP Server 2.1.0 adds tools for retrieving fired alert results, checking alert action status, and finding silent alerts. It also introduces self-service encrypted token management, updated management pages, stronger authentication, and improved telemetry. **What's New** **Alert Investigation** Added three tools for investigating Splunk alerts: * splunk_get_fired_alert_results * splunk_get_alert_action_status * splunk_find_silent_alerts Use these tools to retrieve retained search results for a specific alert firing, check recorded alert action outcomes, and find enabled alerts with no recorded firings. Fired alert results and silent alert discovery support pagination. Silent alert discovery also supports app filtering and a lookback window of up to 90 days. **Encrypted Token Management** * Added self-service token management for non-admin users with the mcp_edit_tokens_own capability. Creating, activating, deactivating, and deleting tokens also requires Splunk’s edit_tokens_own capability. * Users can create, list, activate, deactivate, and delete tokens they create for themselves, and view token status, expiration, and recorded last-use information. * Administrators can manage tokens across users, subject to native Splunk token permissions, and generate or delete the shared encryption key pair. * All encrypted MCP tokens use the public key from this administrator-managed key pair. * Added configurable key expiration, with a default validity of 180 days and a maximum of 365 days. Newly created tokens cannot outlive the key. **Management Interface Improvements** * Updated the Tools page with search, sorting, filters, and bulk activation and deactivation. * Updated the Usage dashboard and changed its default time range to 7 days. * Moved allowed SPL commands and server settings into separate Commands and Server pages. * Added support for Splunk light and dark themes. **Security and Telemetry Improvements** * Strengthened authentication for tool-management operations. * Added token audit events and more context to administrative logs. * Improved logging for SPL errors and failed tool calls. **Issues Fixed** * Fixed splunk_get_indexes to include search-peer indexes while preserving pagination. * Fixed Gemini compatibility with alert severity schemas. * Fixed request recovery after increasing the MCP request timeout. * Fixed an endpoint URL locale mismatch that affected OAuth connections. * Fixed cleanup after failed encrypted-token registration. **Upgrade Considerations** * Direct MCP bearer-token connections now require credentials encrypted with the current server key. Plaintext and previous-key support are removed, along with the require_encrypted_token and legacy_token_grace_days settings. * Existing keys without expiration receive 180-day validity when initialized after upgrade. Existing expiration dates are preserved. * Deactivate all non-expired registered tokens before deleting the shared encryption key pair. After generating a replacement pair, issue new tokens and update clients. * Non-admin users need mcp_edit_tokens_own to access self-service token management and edit_tokens_own to create, activate, deactivate, or delete their own tokens. * Existing tokens are not automatically added to the new registry. The self-service token list shows tokens created by the current user. * Token API integrations must use /services/mcp_token/tokens and /services/mcp_token/key-pair instead of the previous creation and rotation operations at /services/mcp_token. * splunk_find_silent_alerts requires access to \_audit. splunk_get_alert_action_status requires access to the relevant \_internal action logs. * splunk_get_fired_alert_results requires retained search-job results. Expired results are reported as unavailable.


Description:
MCP Server for Splunk Platform The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard and framework that enables seamless, secure, and standardized two-way communication between AI applications (like large language models) and external data sources or tools. It acts as a universal adapter allowing AI systems to access, execute, and integrate functionalities from diverse systems through a common protocol, simplifying data sharing and tool interoperability without custom coding for each integration. Splunk's Model Context Protocol (MCP) server leverages this to provide a standardized, secure, and scalable interface to connect AI assistants, agents, and other intelligent systems with data in the Splunk platform for both Enterprise & Cloud customers in beta. 🔑 Key Features - Universal Connectivity Seamlessly connects AI agents and tools to Splunk data resources in a secure and efficient manner. - Enterprise-Grade Security Includes built-in authentication, authorization, and Role-Based Access Control (RBAC). - Rapid Deployment Offers a plug-and-play solution, eliminating the need for custom integrations. ⚙️ Core Capabilities - Explore the Data Navigate and interact with Splunk data effortlessly. - Discover Knowledge Objects Identify and access relevant saved searches, lookups, and other knowledge assets. - Execute Searches Run powerful Splunk queries to extract insights and drive intelligent workflows. - Leverage AI capabilities from Splunk’s AI Assistant for SPL & MLTK SPL search generation from natural language, search optimization, search explanation, retrieve MLTK models and algorithms.

Description:
DV AI Assistant is an AI-powered security operations application for Splunk designed to help SOC teams investigate security events, generate and execute SPL, and triage Splunk Enterprise Security notable events. The application provides an AI Command Center for natural-language interaction with Splunk data and an AI Triage Center for manual or autonomous notable-event analysis. It supports multiple LLM providers including Ollama, OpenAI, Google Gemini, and custom endpoints, and can use a configurable knowledge base to provide environment-specific context to the AI. DV AI Assistant includes security controls for AI-generated actions and searches. Generated SPL is passed through guardrails before autonomous execution to prevent write or side-effecting commands. IP block and unblock actions require explicit confirmation and the block_ip capability. Built-in admin and sc_admin roles receive this capability by default, while the dv_ai_action role can be assigned separately when block/unblock permission is required. Blocked IP addresses are maintained by the application and exported as a plain-text firewall-consumable list, allowing external firewalls or security controls to retrieve the current block list. The application also includes an autonomous triage worker. When Auto Triage is enabled, the scripted input runs every 60 seconds by default, identifies eligible unprocessed Splunk ES notable events, sends the complete event context for AI analysis, and writes the resulting triage report back to the notable event. Role-based access is provided through dv_ai_user, dv_ai_admin, and dv_ai_action roles. Standard users can access AI Chat and AI Alert Triage, while administrative configuration areas such as AI Providers, Data Context Mapping, Audit, and App Settings are restricted to authorized administrators.

Matching records across several sources, and choosing which source wins each field, are tested but have not yet been run live. Most estates describe the same servers, services and teams in more than one place — a CMDB, a monitoring tool, a list a team keeps — and each is partly right. Adjutant AI can now **reconcile** them: read the sources side by side, decide which records are the same thing, and keep one reviewed view in which every value says which source it came from. It is an administrator feature of the **Enterprise** edition and above, driven through the app's REST interface (`/services/itmip_recon`). A run goes through five steps: 1. **Stage** each source's rows into a holding area. 2. **Accept** a source's data as a whole, or reject it as a whole: enough rows, a usable key on every row, no duplicate keys. A read the source reports as **truncated**, or one that lost more rows than the contract allows, is still accepted for what it saw — but it is never used to decide that something is gone. 3. **Reconcile** the accepted data. Every run leaves a record with a verdict — complete, incomplete or refused — and the reason. 4. **Request and approve.** A complete run becomes the approved view only when **a second administrator** approves it. Approving your own request is refused, and who approved is taken from the Splunk session, never from what the request says. 5. **Promote.** The approved run becomes the current view, and the baseline the next run compares against. **It refuses rather than guesses**, and says why: - When a contract names a holding area for its sources, a reconciliation reads only data that was accepted in step 2, and rows sent with the request are refused. - An organisation's first run is reported as a first run. But if the history of an earlier approved run is missing or cannot be read, the run is refused — starting over would give every record a new identity. - If a source's observation time cannot be read, the run is refused rather than using the time the data arrived. - Two contracts never share a run identity, and one organisation's reconciliation never touches another's. - If one record key turns up as two separate records -- typically two sources of the same kind with no matching rule between them -- the run is not complete and cannot be approved, and the run names the contract gap that caused it. **Lookup tables.** A contract can enrich one source's records from up to two lookup tables (for example a region per team). A lookup table never adds a record of its own, each enriched value names the table it came from, and the run reports how much of the table matched nothing. **Renames.** When a record's key changes and nothing else identifies it, reconciliation treats it as a new record. An administrator can record that the two are the same thing (a *rekey*); a second administrator must approve it, and the old record then keeps its history under the new one instead of being reported as gone. **Freshness and trust per source.** Every run records, for each source, whether it was read recently enough and whether it may report that something is gone — each with a named reason when the answer is no. ### Changed: who may approve a blocked integration write - **Only the person who requested a blocked write, or an administrator, may now see, approve or cancel it.** **Power users can no longer approve other users' runs**; ask the requester or an administrator. The ServiceNow incident and CMDB tools keep their existing `servicenow` licence. ### Sending the reconciled view to ServiceNow (Preview) *Preview.* Writing the reconciled view to ServiceNow is tested against a simulated ServiceNow instance and has not yet been run against a live one. The approved view can now be **written to ServiceNow**, through the same REST interface, in two steps: 1. **Preview** (`dry_run`): what each view would create, update or leave unchanged, record by record. The preview is stored and gets an id. 2. **Go live** (`publish_live`): an administrator names the preview they reviewed. The publication runs only if it would still send exactly what that preview showed; if anything changed since, it is refused and you preview again. Before anything is written, Adjutant asks ServiceNow, without writing, whether each table can be identified (IRE). A table with no identification rule, or one whose records need a host record alongside them, is refused by name. Records are written through IRE, read back, and recorded as owned by the integration. By default only records that changed since the last confirmed write are sent; a full resend (`push_all`) can be requested and is shown in the preview. A table the contract declares read-only is never written. **Removing records.** For a table the integration is authoritative for, a record that is confirmed gone from the sources is **retired** in ServiceNow; a view can opt in to deleting it instead. Only records the integration created and still owns are ever retired or deleted. Retiring uses ServiceNow's CI Lifecycle Management API where it is available to the integration; where it is not, the preview says so ("direct install_status update, lifecycle enforcement bypassed"), approving that preview accepts it, and the run records a warning. Every retirement and deletion is read back. **ServiceNow as a source.** A contract can also *read* a ServiceNow table as one of its sources (`stage_servicenow`): the table is read in full through the organisation's ServiceNow connection, filtered as the contract declares, and staged like any other source; when it is accepted, it takes part in reconciliation. A read that could not finish is still used for what it saw, but never to decide that a record has gone. **A role per table.** The contract declares, for each ServiceNow table it touches, whether the integration is **authoritative** for it (the table must match the reconciled view), only **writes** to it (creates and updates, never removes anything), or only **reads** it. A view takes its table's role from that declaration; a view on a read-only table, a removal on a written table, or two views claiming the same authoritative table is refused before anything is sent, and reported on the reconciliation run. **Held runs.** For a table the integration is authoritative for, a live run is **held** — nothing is written — when the view would publish nothing, when it is the view's first live run, when its output is below the usual size of its recent verified runs, or when it would remove more than 10% of the records the integration owns there (adjustable per view). An administrator approves or rejects the held run (`approve_held` / `reject_held`, naming its preview); who decided, and when, is recorded, and every check is written to the safeguard log. **Checked after every live run.** For an authoritative table, Adjutant reads the table back: the records the integration owns must be exactly the records the view published, field by field. A difference is reported by record and field, and the run is recorded as not verified. Records in the table that the integration does not own are never touched; they are counted and reported. **A recent write test is required.** Before the first live run, and again every 7 days, an administrator runs the write-capability test (`capability_test`): Adjutant writes one test record to a table you name, checks that ServiceNow kept its source attribution, and removes it again. A live run is refused without a passed test younger than 7 days, or when the last verified run is more than 7 days old. ### Changed: a ServiceNow integration reads what its mapping says - **The mapping's filter is applied.** A scheduled ServiceNow integration now reads only the records its mapping selects. Before, the filter could be skipped, so records the mapping excludes (for example retired applications) could be written to the destination. Records written that way by an earlier version stay where they are; remove them yourself if you do not want them. - **Only what changed is read.** After its first run, an integration reads only the records that changed since the last run it verifiably wrote, and its run says so ("no row changed since …"). - **Record values stay out of the AI model.** Adjutant makes the read itself and hands the model a reference to the records, never the records. The model cannot change what is read or what is written. - **The mapping's fields are read.** The fields the mapping lists are requested from ServiceNow, as stored values (for example a status code, not its label). ### Changed: relationships have their own capability test - **Creating relationships is proved before it is relied on.** The capability test can now prove `cmdb_rel_ci`: two probe CIs, a relationship between them, read back exactly and removed again. They are planned for a 2.7.x update. ## 2.5.9 The setup wizard now tells you which model actually answered your question, and says plainly when a gateway publishes no model list, instead of showing a bare error. Where a provider never asks you for a model, the record now adopts the one the checks used, and step 4 shows it before you press Create. A connection now lists **as many Org/BU pairs as you like**: * Naming an **Organisation on its own** covers every Business Unit in it. * Naming **several pairs** makes the connection usable by anyone in any one of them. * Naming **nothing** leaves it open to every Organisation and every Business Unit, which is the default and what most installs want. Both write the same field and the same control is used in both places, because a second implementation of "what did the admin choose" is a second set of rules to get wrong. The short `DFLT` was doing double duty as a real tenant and as the wildcard meaning everybody, so one value meant both. It can be said now. **Nothing changes on upgrade.** A connection saved before 2.5.2 keeps exactly the reach it had: one scoped to an Org still serves that Org, and the shared bootstrap connection stays open to everyone. You only get the new behaviour on connections you edit. Membership is still resolved on the server from the caller's own Splunk roles, never from anything the browser sends, and the explicit per-user and per-role grants continue to work as overrides. --- ## 2.5.1 "The address nobody was asked for" A fix release for 2.5.0, from the first real run of the wizard against OpenAI. ### Choosing OpenAI and pasting a key failed on the first check **If you are on 2.5.0, upgrade.** Choose OpenAI, paste the API key, press test, and the first check failed with `scheme '' is not http or https`, above a paragraph explaining that loopback, private and link-local addresses are refused deliberately so the setup tool cannot be used to scan your network. The old form is still there behind "set it up manually instead", for administrators who already have all twenty three values and do not want to be walked through them. Ten checks run in order, each one budgeted so it finishes inside Splunk Web's own timeout, with a live checklist rather than a spinner. They prove, in order: the name resolves, the route is open, the browser can reach it where that matters, the endpoint is the provider it claims to be, the credential is accepted, the model list is readable, a real question comes back answered, and a real tool call is made and returned. That last pair is the point. A green tick that only means "the key is valid" is what most test buttons give you, and it is why a connection can pass a test and then fail on the first question. The 2.4.0 reliability work rewrote the retry module in place rather than adding to it, which deleted the LLM call orchestrator — while its one caller, the proxy that **every** Ask goes through, still called it. The result was an `AttributeError` on every request, surfaced as a generic internal error with the real reason only in `splunkd.log`. The orchestrator is restored alongside the newer retry helper. The two are disjoint and stay that way: one is the writer's bounded per-request retry, the other is the provider fallback chain with its circuit breaker and per-attempt journal. `tests/test_llm_retry.py` covers the restored path and was failing on `import` for two releases, which is how this reached a release at all. ### Network-policy events were merged, not split When a device snapshot was stored to a Splunk index, every rule from that device arrived as a **single event** containing the whole batch of JSON records, instead of one event per rule. The same applied to the object, warning and snapshot families. Nothing announced it. The field list still showed `rule_id`, `action`, `source_values` and the rest, because Splunk extracts fields from the first JSON object in an event — so the fields you clicked on were real and correct. Only the **count** was wrong, and the counts the app itself reported were counts of records submitted, not of events landed. A `| stats count by device_id` over the rule source type therefore under-reported by however many rules a device had. The cause was a single character. `default/props.conf` declared the parsing rules under `[adjutant:network_policy:*]`, and props.conf applies its wildcard match language to `source::` and `host::` stanzas only — in a source-type stanza the `*` is literal, so the stanza matched nothing and the events fell back to Splunk's defaults. Each family now has its own stanza, and a `[source::itmip_llm_splunk_writer]` stanza backstops any source type added to that path in future. ### A policy field was colliding with one of Splunk's own Expanded policy tuples carry a field named `source` — and `source` is one of the fields Splunk defines on every event, where it names what wrote the record. Splunk does not overwrite on a collision, it **merges**, so `| table source` returned the policy's source address and `itmip_llm_splunk_writer` together in one cell, with nothing to say which was which. Fields whose names Splunk already owns are now written as `original_` — so that one is `original_source`. This applies to the **index** write only: the KV Store rows, the policy graph and the API keep the model's own names, because `source` is part of what a `tuple_id` is hashed from and renaming it there would move every tuple id ever issued. ### `source` and `host` said who wrote the event, not where the data came from Every network-policy event landed with `source = itmip_llm_splunk_writer` and `host = ai_workbench` — true of every event this app has ever written, and therefore no use for filtering or for a CIM-style view of where a policy came from. They now describe the input. `host` is the box the configuration was **read from**: the device or manager when it was reached over the network, and the Splunk instance itself when the input was a file or a paste, because that is the machine that held it. `source` names the input — a file path when the collector recorded one, else the file name, else `cisco:asa:config` for a device configuration or `cisco:fmc:api` for a manager collection. An FMC collection is labelled by the **manager**, not by the device platform it describes, which is the distinction the field is for. ### An Org with its own mapping collection saw an empty one — or someone else's An Org that registers a `mapping_collection` gets its own (`itmip_ai_mappings_`), which is the isolation boundary. The shipped example mappings were only ever seeded into `DFLT`'s, so that collection stayed **empty**: the examples were invisible to the Org, and an integration resolving its `mapping_ref` at run time under that Org found nothing. Compounding it, the Mappings tab did not tell the server which app it was in, so it resolved as the fallback Org and displayed **DFLT's** collection. An admin could Verify and Clear a mapping there, and a schedule running under their real Org would still refuse — pointing at a row in a collection nobody was looking at. The shipped examples are now seeded per Org, and the tab resolves the same Org the runtime does. **One consequence to know about:** mappings authored while the tab was mis-resolving live in the fallback Org's collection. They are not lost, but they belong to that Org and will not appear under yours. Re-create or re-scope anything you need. ### Seeded mappings could never be corrected after the first install A seeded mapping is documented as re-seed-eligible: ship a fix, and an untouched system-owned row picks it up. It never worked. The seeder POSTed to the KV Store collection root, which only ever **inserts** — splunkd answers `409` for a `_key` that already exists and leaves the row alone — and the 409 landed in a bare `except: pass`. Every correction to a shipped mapping since the first install was silently dropped. A second guard compounded it: the seeder skipped any row cleared for unattended use. That was added for a real reason (restarts were resetting clearance) but it froze the whole row rather than the decision, so the mapping most likely to run unattended was the one fixes could never reach. On a real instance the shipped Cisco ASA mapping was still at its pre-B3.3 shape: **no `device_id` in the projection** and **no `source.schema_version`**, so the writer's schema pin had nothing to compare and could not refuse a batch the mapping would silently strip of its NAT view. The refusal that exists to prevent exactly that could not fire. Now: the seeder replaces then inserts, so corrections land; and clearance is carried across an unchanged re-seed but **revoked when the content actually changed**, recording who had cleared it and why it was revoked. A human cleared a specific mapping, not a name — so a changed mapping stops and asks, instead of running under an approval that no longer describes it. ### The shipped ASA Playbook pointed at a superseded mapping "Cisco ASA Policy Ingestion (mapping-driven)" was wired to `cisco-asa-config-to-network-policy-v1`, which is `superseded_by` v2 and pinned to source schema 1.0. The pipeline has emitted 2.0 since the NAT work, so a run through it is refused with `schema_version_mismatch` — and the refusal names v2, meaning the product was telling operators to fix a wiring mistake the product shipped with. The Playbook now names v2. The trailing `-v1` / `-v2` in a mapping name is its **schema generation**, not its lifecycle version; a mapping carries its own `operational v1` separately. Two axes, one letter. The Playbook's mapping picker now shows each mapping's title alongside its ref (the Mappings tab lists them by title, so the same mapping looked like two different objects), flags a superseded choice with the successor's name before you save, and spells out that clearing for unattended is a separate step from promoting. ### Policy records were stamped with the wrong Org and BU Run a network-policy ingestion from the Ask tab in a host app such as `itmip_fis_app`, with the header showing your real Org and BU, and every landed record still said `tenant_org: DFLT`, `tenant_bu: DFLT`. Org and BU are resolved server-side from the caller's roles **and** the app they are working in. The Ask request itself sends that app; the tool dispatch behind it did not, so resolution fell back to the assistant app's own name — which matches whichever Org registered *that* pattern, not the one the user is in. An Org whose `app_patterns` name the host app could never match. The netpol, `splunk_memory` and `splunk_mapping` tool calls now send the host app. This is a context hint, not a grant — an Org matches only when the caller's real roles also match its `role_patterns` — so it cannot widen anyone's access; it makes tenant data land under the tenant it belongs to. Records written on 2.4.0 or 2.4.1 through these tools carry the fallback Org/BU and are not corrected retroactively. **This one is in the frontend bundle**, so hard-refresh the browser after upgrading. ### Security: raw firewall configurations were readable by every authenticated user `itmip_netpol_artifacts` stores collected configurations as base64. Redaction on the import path is opt-in, so unless it was asked for, a stored artifact still contains the secrets the scanner merely counted — on our own sample config, an enable-password hash and two IKEv2 pre-shared keys. That collection had no ACL of its own, so it inherited the app default of `read : [ * ]`. Every protection the artifact store provides — tenant scoping, an owner check, metadata-only reads, a download link that expires in an hour — guards the REST path; a direct KV Store read from a lookup command or the Lookup Editor went around all of it. `itmip_netpol_artifacts`, `itmip_netpol_parses` and `itmip_netpol_snapshots` are now **admin / sc_admin** read and write. No functional change: every netpol read goes through the endpoint's system token, and that endpoint was already admin-gated. The published policy collections (`itmip_network_policy_rules_current` and its siblings) stay readable — they hold modelled policy rather than credentials, and searching them is the product. **If you have run a collection on 2.4.0 or 2.4.1**, treat any credential in a collected config as having been readable by any app user for the artifact's 7-day retention, and rotate accordingly. ### Warnings you can trace back to what they are about A network-policy warning carried `code`, `message` and `line` — a sentence, and no way to go and look. `line` also answers nothing for an API collection, which has objects rather than lines. Warning events now carry `refs{}` (the ACL name, the object id, the uuid an FMC rule referenced — identifiers the parser had already collected and the index write was discarding), `evidence_ref` in the same `#L` form that rules use for `raw_evidence_refs`, and `artifact_id`. One idiom now locates a warning and a rule alike. The offending configuration line itself is still never carried into an index — it stays in the protected, secret-scanned artifact, and the evidence ref is how you reach it. ### Duplicate warnings on the same collection Warnings from an FMC collection are built per rule side, so two access rules referencing the same uncollected port object produced the same warning twice — and the indexed warning event carries `code`, `message` and `line` and nothing else, so the copies were indistinguishable and the repetition told you nothing. Byte-identical warnings now collapse to one; anything that differs, even by a line number, is still two warnings. Warnings are not part of a snapshot's semantic hash, so no snapshot is re-identified by this. ### OCSF telemetry took its timestamp from ingest time `[ocsf:itmip:*]` had the same defect, so agent-telemetry events were timestamped when Splunk received them rather than from the `time` field in the OCSF envelope. On a busy or delayed pipeline that moves events on the timeline. One stanza per OCSF class now. **Upgrading.** These are index-time settings: they apply to events indexed **after** a splunkd restart, and events already in the index stay merged. To correct history, remove the affected events and re-store the snapshots. --- ## 2.4.1 "Getting connected" Everything here came out of two customer setups in the same fortnight: an Azure OpenAI service published through a corporate API gateway, and one behind a private endpoint. The release is about closing the distance between "the test passes" and "it works", and about not making an administrator assemble a URL by hand from three values nobody gave them. ### Find my endpoint (Azure OpenAI) Azure needs the complete address of a deployment, not the address of the service: everything up to and including `/chat/completions`, with the deployment name and an api-version in it. Behind a gateway that address also carries a path prefix chosen by whoever publishes the API. An administrator is typically handed a base URL and expected to work out the other three parts, and getting any of them wrong produces a "Resource not found" that reads like a permissions problem. It checked whether the credential was accepted, and an address that answers "not found" still accepts a credential — so a wrong address passed the test and failed every time it was used. The model that actually answered is now recorded alongside the configured name and used for pricing when the configured name is unknown, so those deployments cost correctly. Where the two differ, both are kept. - **A licence that could never be activated said "re-activate".** A key issued with no device limit records no activations at all, so a node-locked tier can never be satisfied by it and pressing re-activate cannot help. The licence page now says the key was issued without a device limit and needs reissuing, instead of sending administrators round a loop that had no exit. --- ## 2.2.2 "Finish the dashboard" A maintenance release about one thing: runs that did all the work and then ended with nothing on the glass. Existing private playbooks you authored are unaffected; the old entries are retired so you are not offered both. --- ## 2.2.1 "Proven" A maintenance release, and every item in it came from running 2.2.0 against a real estate rather than from reading the code. One new capability came along with the fixes. ### Fraud rings your risk threshold cannot see (Enterprise, fraud-analytics) Risk-based alerting adds up one entity's score across many events. A fraud ring is the opposite shape: many entities sharing one thing. Because those are different questions, no amount of threshold tuning finds a ring. Seventeen mule accounts each earning fifteen points against a threshold of forty are seventeen well-behaved customers, since the risk was split seventeen ways and no single account ever crossed. Lower the threshold and you get seventeen false positives, not one ring. This release adds the query that asks the other question: group by the shared attribute instead of by the account. Imports live on the **Backups** page, which also shows which content version you're currently on — run a backup first and you can roll back in one click. - **Retire without deleting.** A pack can mark an item **retired** — it stays installed but is hidden and switched off everywhere (it can't be picked, run, or used by the assistant). An admin can re-enable it at any time by removing the tag. **Improved — data-quality checks for everyone, and Splunk 10.x readiness.** - **Data-quality ingestion checks are now available on every edition, including the free tier.** Checking whether a feed is actually landing and parsing correctly — on `index=_internal`, through **TrackMe**, and through **Cribl Stream** — is a baseline capability now, not a Professional add-on. - **Ready for Splunk Enterprise 10.2 and 10.4.** The app declares Python 3.9 **and** 3.13 compatibility and has been audited against the 10.x platform changes (dashboards, the web framework, KV Store). Your admin still completes the standard KV Store engine migration as part of any 10.x upgrade. - **Smarter Dashboard Studio building.** The assistant now works from a single, version-aware map of what Dashboard Studio supports on **your** Splunk version — it won't reach for a chart type your version can't render, and when your Splunk is newer than what we've documented it builds conservatively and verifies the result. **Fixed.** - **Fewer false "the dashboard is blank" errors.** A heavy Dashboard Studio dashboard that renders fine but slowly is no longer wrongly reported as blank — the assistant confirms the panels actually returned data before deciding, so it stops wasting a retry on a dashboard that was already correct. A genuinely blank dashboard is still caught. - **TrackMe panels only when they belong.** Fixed a rule that pushed a TrackMe feed-health panel onto every generated dashboard (and used a lookup that fails outside the TrackMe app). The assistant now adds a feed-health panel only when it's actually relevant, using a method that works in your app. --- ## 1.7.0 "ServiceNow integration" (included in the 1.8.0 release) > **Renamed to Adjutant AI.** The app is now **Adjutant AI** (formerly "AI Workbench"). > This is a **display-name change only** — the in-app title (the easter egg now lives on > the dot of the "i" in **Adjutant Ai**), the app label, the documentation, and the > assistant's own self-description all say **Adjutant AI**. Nothing functional changed: > the Splunk app id, your saved searches/dashboards/models, KVStore data, and generated > artifact names are unchanged, so the upgrade is seamless. **New — run playbooks automatically, and from other Splunk apps.** - **On a schedule or on an event.** A playbook can run **unattended** on a schedule (a "morning health check") or in response to a Splunk event — an alert, an ES correlation search, or an ITSI episode. When an event triggers it, the affected thing (the host, user, or entity in the alert) is handed to the playbook automatically, so it investigates exactly what fired. Two ready-made (disabled) examples are included to copy. - **Adjutant AI as a building block for other apps.** Other Splunk AI agents can now ask Adjutant AI to **list** and **run** your playbooks through a small, safe interface (an MCP server). Only playbooks you mark **MCPready** are exposed, every call must name the Org/BU it is for (which must be a business unit you have set up) as a safeguard, and runs go through the same governed, bounded service — never an open door. This interface is **off by default** — turn it on with one setting. When on, the tools can also appear inside **Splunk's own MCP Server**, reachable on the normal Splunk web address (no special port needed); you authenticate with a standard Splunk token. A ready-made, read-only **example playbook** ships enabled so there is always something to see the moment you switch the interface on. **New — "Report an issue" support packaging (all editions).** - One click on any conversation (per-turn 🐞, the Ask panel, or the new **Help tab**) packages exactly what happened — versions, the resolved prompt, the tools and model used, the generated dashboards/searches, and every error and warning — into a single file. - **Safe by construction:** secrets are stripped before anything leaves the browser, and the file is **encrypted** to the support key, so it's safe to send over any channel. - It even **tells you what kind of problem it looks like** and matches known issues, so simple cases are solved without a back-and-forth. - **Send it your way:** download it and attach it to your own ticket, use the built-in support form, or email it. The **Help tab** (Report + Documentation + About) is always reachable — even if the app is locked by licensing. **New — ServiceNow, done properly** (Professional + the `servicenow` feature). Read incidents, changes, problems and the **CMDB/CSDM** in plain English — with bounded blast-radius / dependency traversals ("what's the blast radius if this CI fails?"). Turn a Splunk alert, ITSI episode or ES notable into a rich, deterministically rendered ServiceNow incident and **write the number back** to the originating object (a re-fire updates, never duplicates; the closed-incident policy is configurable). **Security incidents (SIR)** with MITRE ATT&CK, off until an admin enables them. Two transports (REST **or** a ServiceNow MCP server), plus TISC threat-intel enrichment — all server-side and allowlisted, so ServiceNow can never block the assistant. *(Verified against the documented APIs and unit-tested; final certification is on a live ServiceNow.)* **New — run playbooks automatically, and from other apps.** Playbooks can run **unattended** on a schedule, or from a Splunk alert / ES correlation search / ITSI episode (the triggering entity is handed to the run). Adjutant AI can also expose **list / run** over an inbound **MCP server** (off by default, MCPready-only, Org/BU-scoped) — reachable inside Splunk's own MCP Server on the normal web address, with a standard Splunk token. **New — "Report an issue" support packaging (all editions).** One click packages a failing conversation — secret-stripped and **encrypted client-side** — with an automatic problem classification, plus an always-reachable **Help tab** even when the app is licence-locked. **New — Cribl Stream data-quality awareness** (Professional+). Reads Cribl's own forwarded logs and metrics to surface the timestamp / parse / dropped-event problems that happen *inside Cribl, before Splunk can see them* — the "green in Splunk but timestamped wrong" blind spot — folded into one readiness verdict. No Cribl Lake or Search required. **New — LLM reliability: retry, fallback & circuit breaker** (Enterprise). A brief provider hiccup (503 / 529 / rate-limit) auto-retries within a time budget; a per-config **circuit breaker** stops hammering a provider that's down, then probes for recovery; and an ordered **fallback** transparently switches to your next provider (and tells you which it used). Two new admin dashboards — **LLM Health** and **AI Activity** — plus per-user / BU / org concurrency caps, all conservative and off the critical path. **New — live model & cost catalogue (all editions).** Models and prices come from a runtime catalogue that updates without an app rebuild; **automatic model discovery** (Professional+) keeps it current without ever logging your keys; an Enterprise admin screen adds price overrides and manual model registration for private gateways. **Fixed.** Generated Simple XML dashboards now share a single base search across panels (faster) and get a top data-ingestion health panel; corrected a 3× Opus price over-charge (now server-side authoritative, with Opus 4.8 and Fable 5 included). --- ## 1.5.0 "Data Foundation & MCP OAuth" **New:** connect to **OAuth 2.1‑protected MCP servers** (authorization‑code + PKCE for interactive, client‑credentials for unattended; tokens held server‑side, never in the browser — see [MCP_OAUTH.md](MCP_OAUTH.md)); **onboard new data sources** — describe a source or attach a sample file and get a deployment‑ready add‑on package; a **"is my data parsed correctly?"** ingestion/timestamp check that reads Splunk's own internal logs; generated config **validated against your instance** and given a **0–100 Data Quality Score** (A–F); and attach a local sample file in Ask (only the file name is audited, never contents). **Improved:** works with the newest OpenAI "reasoning" models incl. Azure GPT‑5.4 / GPT‑5.4‑mini (auto‑detects the request format); more reliable generated dashboards; generated objects use the **`aiworkbench`** name tag; and Audit‑tab improvements (Business Unit column/filter, local‑timezone timestamps, reliable token/outcome capture). --- ## Earlier releases (1.0.0 – 1.4.3) - **1.4.3** — Clearer guidance and plain-language fixes when a free-tier LLM key hits its provider limits (e.g. Groq token-per-minute caps, Gemini zero-quota keys); the LLM config screen flags these up front. - **1.4.1** — Per-feature capability licensing with edition badges (Professional / Enterprise / MSP); gated features show a padlock, and nothing you created is ever deleted when a tier changes. Turn-level audit logging made reliable; more robust dashboard generation. - **1.4.0** — The assistant reads your own Splunk **live** (real search commands + installed visualizations) instead of guessing; Splunk Security Essentials detection content integrated. - **1.3.3** — TrackMe integration end-to-end (feed-health awareness + actions) with richer built-in platform knowledge. - **1.3.2** — First Splunkbase 1.x release: packaging and permissions hardening. - **1.3.1** — Fixed Org/BU edits dropping fields; safeguard to keep bundled playbooks correct after upgrades. - **1.3.0** — Real, per-Organisation audit logging of every AI interaction (Professional+). - **1.2.0** — Splunk Security Essentials content tools for playbooks. - **1.1.1** — Cisco Deep Time Series Model (CDTSM) playbooks: pre-trained anomaly detection and forecasting via the AI Toolkit, each with a proof dashboard. - **1.1.0** — Multi-tenancy and the Organisation / Business-Unit editor overhauled for clearer, safer tenant scoping. - **1.0.0** — The knowledge layer: ground answers in your organisation's own conventions. *(Releases before 1.0 are early pre-release history and are omitted here.)* --- ## Known issues - **Open the assistant from inside another app.** Adjutant AI is a "host shell": reach it from a navigation-menu entry inside Search, Enterprise Security, ITSI, or your own apps — not by clicking the app tile directly. Everything it creates lands in the namespace of the app you opened it from. - **Some Data Foundation features need self-hosted Splunk.** The configuration-reference grounding and config-package generation (1.5.0) read files on the Splunk server, so they are unavailable on Splunk Cloud; the assistant says so and continues with what it can. --- *When a published fix resolves a tracked GitHub issue, it is summarised here with its issue number — for example: "Fixed: a dashboard panel could display raw HTML markup as text instead of formatting it (#123)."*

The app is not yet publicly downloadable on Splunkbase, and access requests are not currently being accepted. General availability is targeted for fall 2026. Splunk App for Secure Networking helps organizations turn fragmented Cisco infrastructure, networking, identity, security, application experience, and building telemetry into clear executive and operational insights in Splunk. Cisco environments often produce data across multiple products, add-ons, indexes, sourcetypes, and data models. Building a consolidated view normally requires teams to create and maintain separate searches, dashboards, index mappings, and visualizations. This app provides a reusable foundation that brings those signals together through configurable dashboards, shared search definitions, index-mapping macros, health indicators, drilldowns, and interactive topology views. The app includes Secure Networking Posture dashboards covering Zero Trust Access, Secure Infrastructure, Scalable Network Segmentation, Hybrid Mesh Firewalling, and Agentic Operations. It also provides executive briefing, IT health, security, asset inventory, network readiness, building intelligence, Cisco Spaces, and network topology experiences. Searches use configurable index macros instead of hardcoded index names, allowing the app to adapt to different Splunk environments. Administrators can use the included Macro Index Tuning utility to discover relevant data and map dashboards to their indexes. Splunk App for Secure Networking does not collect Cisco data directly. It visualizes data already ingested into Splunk through applicable Cisco add-ons, integrations, and data models. The dashboards displayed and populated in each environment depend on the available data sources. The app is intended for network operations, security operations, IT operations, Splunk administrators, architects, customer success teams, and executives who need a consolidated view of the health, security, availability, and performance of their Cisco environment.

Description:
Collects connection events from a Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center (FMC) over eStreamer and indexes them as sourcetype cisco:sfw:estreamer, with the field names the Cisco Security Cloud app uses for that sourcetype (InitiatorIP, ResponderIP, FirewallRule, AC_RuleAction, ...). Release Notes:
* Security: Built with Go 1.27.3, which refuses server certificates issued by eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authorities revoked for a key compromise * Set `context_window` on every provider to the context length its model is loaded with. The agent now starts summarizing older tool results as a conversation nears it, and sizes the default reply length from it on Anthropic providers and for Claude 4 and later models on Bedrock. Without it, providers on Anthropic's own API and Claude models on Bedrock count as 200,000 tokens and every other provider as 32,768, so a model loaded with less can run out of context * Bug fix: Long investigations re-ran their own searches and could spend their budget without writing an answer, because older tool results were hidden from the model after two rounds. Tool results are now sent in full until the conversation nears the provider's context window, then summarized with the values the agent used * Bug fix: Long answers stopped mid-sentence on Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 through the Anthropic provider, and on Claude 4 and later models on Bedrock, because thinking counts against the 4,096-token default reply length. The default is now 32,000 tokens, or a quarter of the provider's context window when that is under 128,000 tokens, and `default_max_tokens` still overrides it; set it for a Bedrock application inference profile, which keeps Bedrock's default. An answer cut off at that limit, at the model's context window, or by the provider's `request_timeout` while it is being written is kept, says which, and is recorded as truncated in the activity trail; one cut off by the timeout used to fail the turn * Bug fix: One request could make more than a thousand model calls over about an hour, because its limit of 128 calls started again each time a long request continued in the background. The limit now covers the whole request, with one call more only when the background time budget interrupts the last, and that last call writes an answer from what was found so far, saying it was cut short, instead of the request failing with none; an investigation stopped this way writes no decision event, as before * Bug fix: In one investigation the agent could run the same search many times over, each time costing a search. A call identical to an earlier successful one in the same request now gets that result back without running again, the chat marks its card as a repeat, and after three rounds of nothing but repeats the agent is asked for its answer * Bug fix: The Bedrock model list offered base model IDs that Bedrock refuses for current Claude models; it now offers their inference profiles, such as `global.` and `us.`. The docs name the IAM permissions a Bedrock provider needs, including `bedrock:CallWithBearerToken` for a Bedrock API key and `bedrock:ListInferenceProfiles` for the model list * Bug fix: A date given to the agent, such as the "observed 2025-08-01 to 2025-08-14" of a threat report, was refused by Splunk as a search time bound, and the agent searched the last 24 hours instead. A date, a date-time with or without an offset, and Splunk's MM/DD/YYYY now work as `earliest` and `latest`, in the user's Splunk timezone, with `latest` on a date including that whole day * Bug fix: The agent took "now" in the search head's timezone, usually UTC, while Splunk shows each user search results in their own timezone, so it misread the times in results and shifted its relative time ranges by the difference. It now uses the user's Splunk timezone preference (the run-as user's in an alert investigation or `| osai task=`), and the search head's when the user has set none

Release Notes:
* Field conditions after `tx` match key\=value text, such as `status=600`, syslog's `uid=0` or `EventCode=4624`: the fields of an expanded event are the ones Splunk extracts from the original line, key\=value pairs and JSON alike, and no others. * Dates expand as written when a day, hour, minute or second has no leading zero, such as syslog's `Sep 5 00:14:52`. * A timestamp that was already an epoch number expands as that number. * A `tx` search with nothing to narrow on no longer highlights the whole of every event. * After upgrading, run `index=tenx_dml sourcetype=tenx_dml_raw_json earliest=0 | sendalert tenx_dml_to_kv` once, so that templates stored by an earlier version take the date changes.


Short Description:
Send Splunk the logs that sampling and filters keep out to fit the license, on that same license. Compact events take a fraction of the volume and expand back byte-identical at search time; classic dashboards keep their SPL, and one command covers the search bar, saved searches, alerts and the REST API.


Description:
With the Log10x App, Splunk can index compact log events and still search, chart and alert on the original lines. The 10x Receiver stores each event as a template hash plus the values that change, so a stream of repeated patterns takes less of the license. On the OpenTelemetry demo, Splunk's license meter counted 63.91% fewer bytes, encoded events and templates included, and every line expanded back byte-identical with the Receiver settings in the installation steps (measurement: https://github.com/log-10x/benchmarks/tree/main/splunk-license). The same license then holds more: sources that were sampled, filtered or kept out of Splunk to stay under the limit can come back, or the license can be smaller. Classic dashboards keep their SPL: the browser sends each panel's search to the app, which rewrites it on the server. From the search bar, saved searches, alerts and the REST API, a search is wrapped in the tx command (tenxsearch also works). An alert created in the app's Compile Alert view is compiled once into a native saved search, so the scheduler runs no Python. NOT, OR, groups, phrases, field conditions, and values such as IP addresses and hostnames behave as they do on the original data. The 10x Receiver produces compact events, and it is free on up to 10 nodes (https://www.log10x.com/pricing). No sign-up is required to evaluate it: with no license token it runs the full product for 30 days on up to 10 nodes, air-gapped, and a free license removes the time limit (https://doc.log10x.com/manage/license/). The app itself is open source under the MIT license.

Existing TCP/UDP inputs are unchanged; live certificate trust and encrypted delivery require deployment validation. * **Dedicated syslog port suggestions:** New inputs suggest SD-WAN TCP or TLS 9514/UDP 514, ISE TLS, TCP or UDP 9515, and Cyber Vision TLS, TCP or UDP 9516. This setting does not reconstruct missing JSON or establish the cause of a malformed payload. * **TLS syslog input saves:** Sends literal `SSL=true` to the native REST handler for TLS and omits the unnecessary flag for plain TCP. Declares persisted metadata under the platform's native TLS specification, avoiding a custom modular-input classification during Cloud review. Upgrades preserve existing local inputs; invalid plain TCP entries still require correction, and receiver certificates/trust and an enabled TLS handshake remain separate prerequisites. * **ISE alarm severity:** Maps ISE's `CRITICAL` alarm level to `severity=critical`, including retained events, while preserving existing mappings and raw syslog. This is a search-time correction and does not require reindexing or repair malformed API content. * **ISE probe-derived endpoint context (experimental):** `ENDPOINTS_DATA` adds `NAD_ADDRESS`, `ENDPOINT_SOURCE`, `LOGICAL_PROFILE`, and `ENDPOINT_NAME` using bounded Oracle projections. Corrected an unsupported zero-separator requirement that could reject otherwise extractable values. New `ise_probe_diagnostics` explains missing keys, duplicate keys, incomplete headers/values, invalid lengths and unsupported values instead of exposing only `unavailable`. Full inventory collection retains endpoints without RADIUS authentication; raw `PROBE_DATA` remains excluded. Field matching is heuristic and can match embedded field-name text; use the FullReport workflow as the primary NAD source until native format, accuracy, coverage, freshness and largest-cluster performance are validated. * **ISE pxGrid connection tests:** Test Connection now uses the saved or supplied pxGrid client password/certificate for one read-only session service lookup and validates the first provider's HTTPS/8910 URL and trusted hostname using the collector's rules. Missing credentials, rejected access, unavailable services, unsafe/untrusted provider locations, TLS failures and inconclusive responses fail the test with actionable guidance. Added support for Cisco's documented `/pxgrid/mnt/sd` Session Directory route, preserving the node allowlist and rejection of unrelated paths. The check has a ten-second request/deadline budget, a 64 KiB response cap and no automatic retries. It never creates, activates or approves a client. REST and Data Connect results remain visible; individual dataset/Guest/Monitoring permissions and indexed delivery still require collector verification. Password dots are preservation placeholders, not proof of a stored secret. * **ISE pxGrid provider routing:** Session collection accepts the Session Directory route; IP-to-SGT binding collection discovers the SXP provider and sends `getBindings` to its explicitly trusted HTTPS URL instead of the control node. Unrelated provider hosts, unsupported paths and redirects remain rejected. Successful account service discovery does not prove per-service `gets` authorization or provider data access; verify the selected collectors' first polls. * **Illustrated SD-WAN NetFlow guide:** Added customer walkthroughs for v9/HSL and v10/Unified Logging with Manager and Splunk screenshots, separate canary acceptance, HF/downstream verification, troubleshooting and collector-wide capacity measurement. Kept SUL release/policy/resource boundaries and ordinary cFlowd distinct. * **HF validation:** Local configuration readiness is separate from downstream indexed delivery. Forwarding-only hosts default to no indexed-data searches. Detected local or available downstream search can suggest local verification; manual choices remain available. Local searches preserve generating-command syntax and zero results remain unverified. Data Collection Health explains downstream search requirements. Cisco NetFlow package discovery uses the short NetFlow catalog query. * **Search visibility detection:** NetFlow setup and Data Collection Health distinguish downstream search configured, local search only, and search visibility unknown. Local metadata suggests a search location and shows observed peer status and last-check time; manual choices survive refresh. Peer configuration does not prove index access or data arrival. Detection is bounded and launches no search jobs. * **NetFlow listener reset:** Replaced deletion of package-provided Stream stanzas with a verified disabled override and receiver-0-only reset. Other configured NetFlow receivers block reset; unrelated settings, routing, HEC and indexed data remain intact. Errors leave completion unverified. Restart remains operator-controlled. * **Save and host context:** Listener saves change only modified shared settings and verify readback. Rejected input updates identify partial saves without rendering raw server error pages. Search visibility also shows the host and reported Splunk roles, separately from search access or delivery proof. * **Health dashboard layout:** Deployment context and search visibility appear below the tabs and filters in a section collapsed by default. The heading retains the search visibility status; expand it for deployment details and refresh. Product cards now show one status combining freshness and collection findings: partial or unverified coverage is amber; persistent failures are red. **View details** includes affected inputs and expected sourcetypes alongside freshness evidence. Multi-sourcetype report lists remain complete, and dialogs stay above the sidebar on narrower screens. * **Support bundle source and streaming:** Search heads and hosts with an available downstream peer default to indexed logs; forwarding-only hosts without that search path default to local TA files. The source remains selectable. Full exports compress logs as they are processed, removing the cumulative uncompressed-size cutoff while retaining the 50 MiB compressed, one-million-event and five-minute limits. Versioned worker assets avoid stale support-export code after upgrades; refresh open pages. * **Local bundle diagnostics:** Failed local file reads show their HTTP status when available. A ZIP with no log events and unavailable log sections is explicitly labeled configuration-only rather than showing a successful log collection message. * **Support bundle recovery:** When local file collection is unavailable, the dialog explains how to install the TA on a search head with access to the HF’s forwarded TA logs in `_internal` and generate an indexed bundle there. Release Notes:
Version 1.4.0 carries the 1.3.0 changes as well, which were never published separately, so an upgrade from 1.2.1 lands both sets at once. NEW: three saved searches an AI agent can call by name. PolySwarm Indicator Lookup takes one indicator and returns one row. PolySwarm Indicator Lookup with Attribution adds malware family and actor at up to double the cost. PolySwarm Quota Remaining reports what is left and spends no indicator quota. They exist so an AI agent reaching Splunk through an MCP server can use this app without an administrator registering a custom tool or editing an allowlist. All three ship disabled. Two of them spend a metered request every time something dispatches them, so turning them on is a deliberate act: Settings, Searches reports and alerts, with the App filter and the Owner filter both set to All, then Enable from the row's Edit menu. They carry no schedule, so enabling one starts nothing. NEW FIELD: polyswarm_status, on both lookup searches, reading answered, not_found, refused or error. A lookup that failed used to be indistinguishable from a value PolySwarm has no record of. It is not any more. NEW FIELD: daily_api_metered, on the account row. An unmetered plan reports a daily limit of zero beside a remaining count that reads as nothing left and means no cap. This field says which it is. FIXED: the command now reads its credential and its configuration in this app's namespace. Running polyswarmsearch from another app, the Search app included, failed with an error saying no API key was stored. That is the first thing many customers tried. FIXED: a missing API key reported a Python file path and a line number. Every command now names the setup page instead. CHANGED, AND IT CHANGES A PUBLISHED FIELD: PolyScore is no longer published for a URL, a domain or an address. The column is still there and it is empty on those rows. The platform returns the same score for every URL artifact whatever the detection engines reported, so a convicted host read as benign. Read the verdict and the detection counts for those indicator types. If you alert, rank or report on PolyScore for URL, domain or address indicators, review those rules before upgrading. CHANGED: certificate verification on the app's connection to splunkd is now an administrator setting, and it ships off. Splunk ships an environment variable that disables verification outright, so the setting makes the choice visible rather than assumed. RENAMED: the app is now PolySwarm Malware Reputation and Sandbox. The app id, the directory, every command, every field name and every saved object are unchanged, so an upgrade carries everything over. Tested on Splunk Enterprise 10.6.0.5. Supported on 9.4 through 10.6 and on Splunk Cloud Platform.


Short Description:
PolySwarm malware reputation, sandbox detonation and file reputation for Splunk Enterprise and Splunk Cloud. Hash lookup and IOC enrichment for MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, URLs, domains and IP addresses: crowd-sourced verdicts from many engines, malware family attribution, an opt-in threat intel feed, a matching search and three saved searches an AI agent can call.


Description:
PolySwarm Malware Reputation and Sandbox integrates crowd-sourced malware threat intelligence into Splunk by enriching indicators of compromise, or IOCs, with verdicts derived from multiple detection engines. It is a file reputation and hash lookup source for the SOC: the app processes MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-256 hashes, URLs, domains and IP addresses found in Splunk events, annotating them with verdicts, detection counts and malware family attribution sourced from the PolySwarm platform. It extracts and refangs indicators from raw text fields within the search head environment, at no cost and with no API key, and submits URLs to a cloud-based sandbox for behavioral analysis. The app operates entirely on the search head tier and relies on a key-value store to cache verdict data, track sandbox task state, and maintain modular input checkpoints. Enrichment occurs through five specialized search commands that query the PolySwarm API: the indicators being looked up are sent to PolySwarm, and nothing else from the deployment is transmitted. A local verdict cache means a repeated indicator costs nothing, and every metered request carries an explicit ceiling. Search heads that reach the internet through a proxy can route this traffic through it, with credentials held in encrypted storage and certificate verification on the PolySwarm connection always enforced. Events tagged with the polyswarm:artifact source type represent threat intel pulled from the PolySwarm feed and from sandbox task results, and each one carries the artifact's MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-256 so it can be matched against events however your own sources log a digest. Four saved searches ship and all four ship disabled. PolySwarm Indicator Match correlates the indexed feed against your own events and carries the verdict, detection counts, family attribution and report link through to the alert, so an analyst sees why a match matters rather than only that one occurred; it reads indexed events only and spends no PolySwarm quota. The other three are for an AI agent reaching Splunk through an MCP server: PolySwarm Indicator Lookup answers for one indicator, the same search with Attribution adds family and actor, and PolySwarm Quota Remaining reports what is left without spending indicator quota. Two of those three spend a metered request per run, which is why enabling them is a deliberate administrative act. Every answer carries a status field reading answered, not_found, refused or error, so an automated caller never has to read English to learn whether a lookup failed or the platform holds no record. Three dashboards cover enrichment activity and entitlement, sandbox detonations, and per-indicator triage. Opening any of them spends nothing. Four workflow actions give an analyst one-click enrichment from a search result's field menu, enrichment with attribution, navigation to the PolySwarm portal, and the triage page opened on that indicator.

Description:
Kubernetes Search brings live, read-only access to the Kubernetes API into the Splunk search bar. Instead of switching to a terminal and kubectl, you run SPL - | k8s kind=pods namespace=payments - and Splunk queries the cluster's API server directly and streams the current state into your search. The problem it solves: when something breaks in a cluster, the question is usually "what is true right now?" - is the pod still crash-looping, what do its events say, is the node Ready. Answering that has meant leaving Splunk, holding cluster credentials, and running kubectl by hand. Ingestion pipelines give you history, but at the cost of storage and license volume, and they show the cluster only as of the last sample. Kubernetes Search answers the live question from inside Splunk, with no credentials handed out and every query recorded in the Splunk audit log. How it works: - Five search commands cover the common kubectl verbs: | k8s (list or get any resource), | k8slogs (stream pod logs), | k8sevents (cluster events), | k8sdescribe (an object plus its events), and | k8syaml (format JSON as YAML). - Everything runs on the search head and is strictly read-only - it never applies, scales, or deletes anything. - Nothing is indexed: no storage cost, no license volume, no source types, no field extractions. Results exist only for the life of your search. - Register many clusters and fan out with context=* - each row carries a cluster field, so you query and aggregate across your whole fleet from one pane. - Access is gated by a Splunk capability and a per-cluster credential model (shared, per-user, or Kubernetes impersonation), so analysts get controlled, audited read access without being handed kubectl or cluster credentials. - A short-lived on-disk cache keeps dashboards from hammering your API servers; Secrets are never cached. There is no agent to install in your cluster - only a network route from the search head to the API server and a credential. The app installs on search heads only and writes nothing to any index. It pairs naturally with ingestion: use Monitoring Kubernetes or OpenTelemetry for history and trends, and Kubernetes Search for the live picture - in the same Splunk session. Kubernetes Search runs on a free tier with no license key (one user and one cluster, on a single standalone search head). A paid license, priced per user, covers your whole team and unlocks multiple clusters, search head clustering, per-user credentials, and impersonation. Built and supported by Outcold Solutions. item.description:

New * MITRE ATT\&CK on every event. DarkStrata now labels each credential exposure with the ATT\&CK techniques it evidences. The add-on extracts them into mitre\_technique\_id, mitre\_technique and annotations.mitre\_attack on both sourcetypes, deduplicated per bundle. * ATT\&CK annotations on all four Enterprise Security correlation searches (mitre\_attack: T1555.003 and T1589.001 on the infostealer searches, T1589.001 on the third-party and critical exposure searches), so notable events and risk objects carry techniques. Short Description:
Ingest DarkStrata credential-exposure threat intelligence into Splunk and Enterprise Security. Detect compromised credentials, infostealer infections and third-party exposure in real time, with CIM-compliant data, ES correlation searches and adaptive-response actions.


Description:
DarkStrata Threat Intelligence Add-on for Splunk brings DarkStrata's credential-exposure intelligence directly into Splunk and Splunk Enterprise Security (ES), so your SOC can detect and respond to compromised credentials before they're used against you. DarkStrata continuously monitors breach data, infostealer/malware logs and third-party exposure for credentials tied to your organisation. This add-on pulls that intelligence into Splunk as structured, CIM-compliant events - ready for correlation, alerting, dashboards and automated response. Use it to: - Detect compromised credentials before they're used maliciously - Identify malware infections through infostealer credential detection - Monitor third-party risk by tracking corporate credentials exposed on external sites - Automate incident response via ES notable events, correlation searches and adaptive-response actions - Enrich threat hunting with credential-exposure context Data is delivered in STIX 2.1 format and mapped to the Authentication and Threat Intelligence CIM data models, so it works out of the box with Enterprise Security's threat-intelligence framework. Collection is incremental and checkpoint-based - only new intelligence is fetched on each run - with configurable batching, rate limiting and connection pooling for predictable performance.

Short Description:
Render arbitrary HTML inside a Dashboard Studio panel. Supports `{{field}}` interpolation from search results, theme-aware CSS variables, inline SVG, and optional (off-by-default) script execution. Ideal for branded headers, status badges, rich tables, callouts and bespoke layouts Studio can't otherwise produce.


Description:
Dashboard Studio's markdown panel is deliberately limited — no styled spans, no inline SVG, no data-driven HTML. **HTML Renderer** fills that gap with a custom visualization that renders a HTML template you control, optionally populated from your search results. Use it for branded dashboard headers, "● LIVE" status badges, colour-coded callouts, custom legends, KPI ribbons, inline SVG diagrams/floor-plans, and any rich layout the native panels can't express. Values from the primary data source can be injected with simple `{{field}}` placeholders, so the HTML can reflect live search results (e.g. `Last update: {{latest_time}}`). The renderer is **theme-aware** — it exposes Splunk's CSS variables so your markup automatically matches light/dark dashboards. Script execution is **disabled by default** and only enabled via an explicit, clearly-labelled "Allow Scripts (DANGEROUS)" option, so the default behaviour is safe static HTML. Standard `studio_visualization` custom viz, dependency-free.

Description:
**Airspace Radar** turns a table of aircraft positions into a live, animated radar scope inside Dashboard Studio — a rotating phosphor sweep, range rings, centre cross-hair, per-aircraft callsign labels and heading vectors. It's a striking way to present ADS-B / flight-tracking data, geospatial point movement, or any "things on a scope" dataset. The data contract is simple: **one row per aircraft**, with fields `hex`, `callsign`, `lat`, `lon`, `altitude_ft`, `heading`, `speed_kts`. Drive it from a live ADS-B feed (it pairs naturally with the companion **TA-airspace-watch** modular input that polls a tar1090/dump1090 receiver), from historical flight data, or from any search that produces those columns. item.title: Custom Viz - Realtime Clock - v1.0.8 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
Release notes: https://github.com/livehybrid/viz-realtime-clock/releases/tag/v1.0.8


Short Description:
Two animated clock visualizations for Splunk Dashboard Studio: a smooth **analog** clock face (with optional digital readout) and a seven-segment **digital** LCD clock. Timezone-aware, themable colours, optional phosphor glow. No data required — drop one on any dashboard for a live, always-current clock.


Description:
Dashboard Studio has no built-in clock, yet operations walls, NOC status boards, world-clock panels and "as of now" headers all want a live, ticking time display. **Realtime Clock** adds two purpose-built custom visualizations that render the current time entirely client-side at 60fps — no streaming data, no scheduled searches, no backend. **Analog Clock** — a smooth analog face with sweeping hands, tick marks, an optional digital readout and day/date line, and a configurable phosphor glow. Hand, second-hand and tick colours are all configurable. **Digital Clock** — a seven-segment LCD-style display with a blinking colon, 12/24-hour modes, optional seconds, a date line, ghost (unlit) segments for an authentic LCD look, and a phosphor glow. Both support **local time, UTC, or any IANA timezone** (e.g. `Europe/London`, `America/New_York`, `Asia/Tokyo`), so a single dashboard can show a row of world clocks. Because the time is computed in the browser, the clocks stay accurate to the second regardless of search refresh intervals. Built as standard `studio_visualization` custom viz, themable to light/dark, and dependency-free.

\- The index-time settings for Webex data have moved out of this app into a new add-on, TA\_sideview\_webex. Install it wherever Cisco's Webex add-on runs its inputs. Without it you will be affected by several bugs. For example long meeting quality records would be cut off at 10,000 bytes and lost. \- Fixed call\_id for Webex calls, which was different on every leg, so a forwarded or simultaneous-ring call showed as several calls. call\_id now comes from the Correlation ID, which all legs of a call share. \- A meeting's schedule, the meeting itself and its quality records now share one call\_id, and the meeting usage and attendee reports now appear in Investigate Calls. \- The duration on meeting usage and attendee reports is now in seconds, like every other duration in the app, rather than whole minutes. \- A scheduled meeting now shows as one row with the meeting that took place. A scheduled meeting nobody joined shows on its own, with no participants. \- New fields connected\_at and disconnected\_at, so that concurrency and duration\_elapsed in Investigate Calls now work for Webex calls and meetings, where they were always empty. \- Worked around a Splunk defect in which a field that Webex reports as an empty string could make stats list(), values() and dc() silently drop values, or run two values together separated by a semicolon. Any panel that listed or counted such a field - serverRegion, clientType, osType and a number of others - could show both the wrong values and the wrong number of them. Those fields now arrive absent rather than empty, which Splunk handles correctly. One visible change: a value that used to appear as a blank is now simply not there.
